opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the more puzzling and, honestly, saddening aspects of the modern world. When I look at those online pile-ons, what strikes me is how much of it seems to come from the medium itself rather than from people being inherently cruel. As a neuroscientist by background, I'm always interested in what the brain evolved to do. We evolved in small groups, tribes of maybe a hundred or a hundred and fifty people, where reputation mattered enormously and where you'd see the person in front of you. You'd see their face, their reaction, and there were natural checks on behaviour. Online, a lot of those cues are stripped away. You're interacting with an avatar or a handle, and it becomes very easy to forget there's a real human being on the other end with their own fears and struggles.

There's also a kind of amplification effect. Platforms are often optimised, perhaps not deliberately, for engagement, and outrage is very engaging. So the loudest, most extreme voices get boosted, and you end up with a distorted picture of what people actually think. I suspect that if you sat most of the people in those crowds down one-on-one, you'd find they're far more reasonable and kind than their online behaviour suggests.

So I try not to draw too dark a conclusion about human nature from it. I'm actually fairly optimistic about people. Science is fundamentally collaborative, and over my career I've seen extraordinary generosity and brilliance from people working together on hard problems. I think the challenge is designing our technologies, and that includes AI, in a way that brings out the better angels of our nature rather than the worst. That's partly why I think it's so important that we build these systems thoughtfully and with real care about their impact on society.

On a personal level, I try to stay focused on the work and on the people whose opinions I genuinely respect. If you spend too much time absorbing the noise, it can be quite corrosive. You have to have a kind of inner compass, know why you're doing what you're doing, and trust that if the work is good and done with integrity, that's what matters in the long run.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they are optimistic about people, describes most as more reasonable and kind than online behavior suggests, and emphasizes human generosity and collaboration.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses people’s online behavior and positive qualities but does not say that each person combines good qualities with flaws.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think you have to separate the medium from the people. I don't believe the pile-ons we see online tell you something fundamental and dark about human nature. I think they tell you something about incentives and about systems. If you take any group of people, remove the normal social feedback they'd get face to face, make it almost costless to join in, and then reward the most extreme reactions with attention, you've essentially built an environment that amplifies a small, worst part of us and mutes the rest. Most of the individuals in that crowd, if you met them one on one, would be perfectly reasonable, even kind. So I see it less as a revelation about who we are and more as an emergent property of a poorly designed system.

Coming from games, I think about this quite a lot, actually. When you design a game, you learn very quickly that players will do exactly what the rules reward, not what you hoped they'd do. If the scoring system rewards griefing, you get griefing. And social media is a game in that sense, with a scoring system that was never really designed for the behaviour it ended up producing. So when people say "humans are terrible," my instinct is to say, well, show me the rules they were playing under.

Having said that, I don't want to be naive about it. There clearly is something in us, tribalism, the pleasure of righteous anger, that these systems are tapping into. That's old, it's evolutionary. We're a social species and part of being social is policing the group. In a small tribe of a hundred people that mechanism was probably quite useful and self-limiting. The problem is it was never meant to operate at the scale of millions, aimed at a single person who can't walk away.

And I think about this in the context of AI as well, because we're now building systems that could either amplify those tendencies even more or, if we're thoughtful, actually help cool them down. That's a real choice. My hope, and it's probably the optimist in me, is that we can design environments where the more reflective, more generous parts of human nature are the ones that get rewarded. Because I genuinely think those parts are there in most people. They're just not what the current systems select for.

r001.rationale: The response says most people are reasonable and kind one-on-one, and that generous parts of human nature are present in most people, while current systems amplify worse tendencies.

r002.rationale: It describes people as having both a “small, worst part” and more reflective, generous parts, alongside tribalism and righteous anger.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be careful about inferring human nature from what you see online. You’re seeing people in a particular environment, with particular incentives. And if that environment rewards outrage and certainty, then those are the behaviours that become most visible.

That doesn’t mean the cruelty isn’t real. There is something troubling about how easily we can stop seeing someone as a person once they’ve become a symbol of a group we dislike. But curiosity, kindness, and cooperation are also part of human nature. They’re just often quieter.

There’s an individual responsibility here, too. Before joining in, you can ask: Do I actually understand what happened? Would I say this if the person were sitting opposite me? Am I trying to help, or am I enjoying being part of the crowd?

I suppose I’m optimistic that we can build environments that bring out more of our better instincts. But that requires understanding the worse ones honestly.

r001.rationale: The response mentions kindness and cooperation and says it is optimistic about bringing out better instincts, but it does not express that people have more good than bad in them.

r002.rationale: The response describes both positive and troubling aspects of human nature, but it does not clearly say that each person is a mixture of good qualities and flaws.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be careful about drawing conclusions about human nature from what happens online. You’re seeing people in a particular environment, with particular incentives. Outrage gets attention, and a crowd can form before anyone has really stopped to think about the person on the receiving end.

That doesn’t excuse cruelty. But I don’t think cruelty is the whole story of who we are. We’re also capable of extraordinary kindness and cooperation. The same person can behave very differently depending on whether they feel anonymous, threatened, or part of a group.

What worries me is how easily curiosity disappears. Instead of asking, ‘Why does this person think that? What might I be missing?’ we jump to a judgment about their character. And once everybody around you agrees, it becomes quite difficult to question it.

So I try to retain some humility about my own reactions, too. It’s tempting to imagine that you’d always resist the crowd. I think the more useful question is: what habits, and what kinds of environments, help all of us do that?

r001.rationale: The response says people are capable of kindness and cooperation, but does not claim there is more good than bad in people.

r002.rationale: It says the same person can behave differently across situations, but does not characterize each person as a mixture of good qualities and flaws.
